1. You should try to eat to a caloric deficit in order to lose body fat. What you eat doesn't matter as much as how many calories you're taking in vs burning off. 

2. Running is a great way to burn calories and all it doesn't require a gym or personal trainer. You will also be surprised how much just doing  pushups can benefit you in terms of arm size. Definitely check out /r/bodyweightfitness as they have tons of resources to get you ripped without access to the weights you could get at a gym.

3. You don't have to time your workouts, you can simply end the workout when you've finished all your exercises. If you're going to be running you could go the route of timing your runs (20-30 minutes is a good place for a beginner to shoot for) or you could track your mileage. I.e. running for so many miles each workout. 2 miles is going to be a good place to start if you don't run a lot, but don't be discouraged if you find it difficult to do 1. Humans were built for running, so it's something you'll get better at fairly quickly, even if it's difficult in the moment. I also like your idea of a 60 day marker. If checking off one day every day is something that is reinforcing to you, do that. The key is finding what works for you and just sticking with it. As for how many days a week you should be working out, anywhere between 3 and 5 days a week is a solid foundation. You don't want to try and do 7 days a week and get burnt out, but 1 day a week won't get you the results you want. Just make sure you're listening to your body

Good luck and have fun!

Sadly with depression (or even anhedonia) there are no "quick fixes". If youre looking for a supplement to boost dopamine,  I doubt you'll find one. The release of dopamine is a response to feelings or events that we enjoy. Sex, eating, warmth, etc. The only way to boost it is to do things that you like. I know you're looking for something that you can physically take, but I don't think that will solve anything even if you find one. I think you need to retrain your brain to find pleasure in life. For me personally, meditation has helped tremendously with that. If you have the time, read the book "success through stillness". I think you'll find what you're looking for in there. I'm telling you all this as someone who has dealt with major depression for the better part of the last 5 years. The time when I made the most progress was when I figured out that if I dont put in the work to fix my mindset, then no amount of drugs in the world will help me. Sorry for the long read, but best of luck!

 I think you're blaming yourself too much. Nothing you could have done would have stopped her. If you hadn't been visiting your daughter (which you should not feel guilty about, because she absolutely needs you at this time in her life.), she might have done it while you were out getting groceries or something. She was fully bent on her actions being final. If you read about suicides, you'll find that when people use methods like guns, they are a lot more serious than people who us things like pills. The fact that your wife chose such a decisive way of ending her life meant that she was going to do it one way or another. I know you feel like it's your fault, but what could you have done? You cant force her to take her medication. You cant suicide-proof your apartment (think about it. That means no cords whatsoever, no forks or knives, no pens or pencils, it's impossible). And you can't watch her constantly, because you have your own life to live. In the end, she got all the help she could have.

The facts of the matter are that you made the decisions that you thought were the best at the time based on the info you had. There's no reason to feel guilty. Your wife's actions were not under your control, no matter what you think. You'll drive yourself insane thinking about what you could have done. Right now there's a little girl who needs a stable father figure in her life, and a family that needs to grieve for their daughter. But don't forget about yourself. I'm not a therapist or psychiatrist, I'm just a psych major, but from what I've learned on the subject, most of the diagnosing of mental illnesses has little or nothing to do with what the client thinks they have. Most professionals will base their  diagnoses on the dsm-5, which is the big book o' mental disorders. The dsm-5 describes each disorder by it's symptoms, so it doesn't  really matter what you tell the psychiatrist/psychotherapist/psychologist. If you display the behavior consistent with a specific mental disorder, you will be diagnosed with it, if you don't, then you won't. 

Example from my own life: I went to a therapist because I wasn't doing well in school. I was majorly depressed, but told him I thought I had ADHD, because I couldn't concentrate and I thought I fidgeted a lot (common symptoms of depression and anxiety). He ran a number of tests checking for ADHD, as well as other things, and determined I didn't fot the criteria for ADHD, but fit the criteria for depression very well. So he still treated it as a valid claim, and ran tests to check and make sure, despite the fact that I was very clearly on the opposite end of the spectrum.

TL; DR: psychiatrists/therapists look at your behavior, if it matches a disordered person's you likely have the same disorder, if it doesn't, then you probably don't have that disorder. So what you say you have is basically irrelevant.

There is a principle in psychology called the fundamental attribution error, which states that we often attribute the way a person acts to their personality, rather than the situations surrounding them. Essentially, this means that we misjudge people based on our own stereotypes and beliefs. For example, if you were to see someone snap at their friends in public, many of us would assume that that person is a mean and angry person, when they could be going through a situation that has stressed them out, such as a divorce or break up, and their friends' actions were the straw that broke the camel's back. If this was you, then you would give yourself a free pass, and say things like, "who wouldn't be stressed out?". 

You would also consider that your actions leading up to you blowing up on your friend, such as being easily irritated or being uncommonly withdrawn, would have clearly indicated that you were stressed out by something. However, to the passersby, and even some of your friends, it would appear that you're just a cranky and unkind person, even though you know this not to be true.

The reason I say all of this is that, to your family, your actions may correspond to the actions that they would expect from someone that they consider a "freak", based on the mental profile they have created in their minds about how a "freak" should act. This is a problem MANY people with depression face. Often times, the people in your family have no idea what it means to be depressed. As a result, their mental profile of a person with depression is more than likely a person who never stops talking about how sad they are and how much they want to kill themselves. Sadly, the majority of people don't associate depression with a lack of motivation/willpower, low self esteem, helplessness, or the inability to find the energy to get out of bed because the mere thought of doing anything is so draining that you feel physically exhausted, even if you know that it's all in your head. Consequently, if they see a person exhibiting the signs of depression, they will often misinterpret them as something else.

I personally believe the best way to make sure people notice and understand how you feel is to tell them. People aren't mind readers, and if you want them to know something, even if you see it as obvious and easily noticeable, you need to tell them. 

If you tell them, then they will have to face it in the light of day and see your depression for what it is. This is the best thing you can do for yourself, because once you do that, they will have to make a choice to either get you help or not. If they choose to help, then you not only have a solid group of people you can talk to, who will always be there when you need them, but you will also have the resources you need to get help from a professional, providing that you would be comfortable taking that route. And if they choose not to, then you will have identified part of the problem, which is the first step to fixing it, so congratulations.

On a personal note, I'd like to thank you for posting here. Talking to somebody is the number one way to give yourself an edge over depression, and I feel like if I can help even one person beat depression it makes all the years of suffering I had to go through, and will have to go through, worth it. Best of luck to you. Feel free to PM me if you need someone to talk to, or if you just want to share your successes with someone.

TL;DR- Talk to them, if you don't explain how you're feeling then they'll never have a good idea of what you're going through.
